concepts.hook: A bone needle Ennu dropped on the shore after stitching the first sail, so the sky's torn places are still sewn shut from this Reach.
A carding comb of driftwood teeth whose seven gaps are the gusts that tease the northern pass into wool.
A grey stone weight that keeps the trawl down, and that sits low in the Reach and will not rise however hard the wind pulls.
A fishwife's knife, bright at the edge where she cut her own hand, and still kept sharp by the cold stars around it.
The grit-stone the Gale wets to sharpen his squalls, and the faint band of cloud beside it is the spray that never dries.
A punch for lacing sailcloth, its ring of small stars the eyelets it leaves, and every boat-mender in the islands knows its pattern.
A withy ring hung with running loops for taking gulls at the feast, left open and empty now as a warning to the greedy.
A hood waxed against rain, first worn by the wife of the first kite-maker, and seen in the sky as a dark cap of stars over the Reach.
Two knitted mittens a girl made for a boy out on the water, one given in courtship and the other still waiting in the sky.
A cap tied under the chin with long ribbons, a sign of a betrothal accepted, whose streamers are a line of stars that trail toward the north.
A sleeve ripped on the bird-cliffs and patched with a different cloth, kept as a sign that a mended thing can still hold wind.
The round opening in the roof where the hearth smoke leaves, a ring of stars that the Reach's grandmothers watch to know if the house will be warm.
A frame of lashed driftwood where split cod hang in the wind, its rungs a row of pale stars that the Gulls count each evening.
A shallow vat where brine is pressed from the catch, a white stain across the sky that the sailors use to judge the season's luck.
A whalebone cup passed hand to hand at weddings, so that the sky is always carrying one drink from one person to the next.
A single oar that a man set down to go kiting and never came back for, which is why it still rests at the edge of the Reach.
A skin boat shaped like a gull in flight, used by young men to row out to a girl's cliff, and its bow-star points at the rocks where she waits.
A fish-trap basket with nothing in it, a cluster of gaps among the stars that marks a catch the sea kept back.
The small kite flown over the bay for a child lost to the water, its tail a line of knotted cloth so the child can follow it up.
A kite flown by a courting pair, each holding one line, with the knot between them where the two strings meet at the sky's edge.
A kite with no bell on its line, sent up to ask the wind a question that must not be answered in sound.
A weather kite hung with a bone bell that rings when the wind turns, so the stars of its frame are said to wait for the first chime.
A kite shaped like a hunting bird, flown above the nets to frighten off the gulls, and it hangs over the Reach with its wings spread wide.
A kite that carries a lead weight on its tail to measure how high the wind stands, its string a plumb line dropped from the pole.
A mourning kite with a tail of black wool, flown the morning after a death so the dead can see the way up to Vel.
A kite whose tail is tied with one knot for every winter survived, a tally Hesk keeps in the Reach where the children learn to count.
A kite whose sail was torn in a storm and sewn back by a widow, its patch a pale square of stars that the Reach's makers point to for luck.
A plain white kite raised at a wedding so the wind can bless the couple, its tail trailing down toward the bride's new house.
A kite that carries a small oil lamp up the line on still nights, so that boats coming in from the Leeward dark can find the harbour.
The clay pot of lamp-fat set by the door, a small warm knot of stars that the Reach's households light first when the nights grow long.
